The Distributional Consequences of Net-Zero Transitions (with Hakkı Yazıcı)
Working Paper · Slides · Submitted

This paper studies the distributional consequences of net-zero transitions. Using an environmentally-extended input-output table linked with the US Consumer Expenditure Survey, we show that the carbon intensity of expenditure declines with income but rises with age, largely due to differences in energy expenditure shares. We develop a heterogeneous-agent overlapping-generations model with non-homothetic preferences and age-dependent energy needs that matches these patterns. We evaluate a carbon tax path consistent with the U.S. net-zero target under the Paris Agreement. We find that, although higher energy prices disproportionately affect poorer and older households in the short run, lifetime welfare costs are broadly similar across income groups and display a U-shape over age, with middle-aged cohorts most affected. Crucially, these distributional outcomes depend on the timing of carbon taxes: front-loaded paths are more regressive and hurt older households more, while back-loaded paths shift the burden toward middle-aged cohorts and richer households.

Skills That Stay: Mobility and Human Capital Investment Across the Skill Distribution

In the canonical Rosen-Roback model of location choice, workers are freely mobile, so person-based investments such as education and training are orthogonal to place-based policy. In practice, workers have strong preferences for living near where they grew up, which means human capital investments also function partly as place-based policy. Existing work has studied this almost exclusively in the context of college expansion, a policy that causally increases mobility and so generates substantial brain drain. This paper uses the Longitudinal Educational Outcomes (LEO) dataset, which links administrative records for the universe of English students from school into employment between 2003 and 2024, to study the spatial incidence of human capital investment across the whole skill distribution. Preliminary results point to meaningful differences in where the returns to investment accrue across the skill distribution, with implications for the design of place-based policy

title: Public goods
text:
A few bits of code I’ve written over the years for fairly standard tasks that were annoying and time-consuming. I am confident in the accuracy of the code for my specific purposes, but no warranty whatsoever is offered for use elsewhere.

Data cleaning

Cleaning the Consumer Expenditure Survey

Stata code that cleans the CEX following Aguiar and Bils (2015). Handles top-coding, multi-quarter aggregation across the interview and diary surveys, and the 2013 redesign. Outputs a household-quarter panel with consistent expenditure categories from 1996 onward.


Cleaning the PSID

R code that cleans the PSID following Guvenen and Smith (2014). Constructs annual measures of earnings, wealth, and consumption with consistent definitions across the biennial waves post-1997.



Geography

Linking historical UK geographies

A Bash + Python pipeline that uses the ONS Geography Portal to crosswalk administrative geographies across boundary changes — parishes, wards, and LSOAs — with population-weighted apportionment for variables that don’t aggregate cleanly.
